data.title: Why Estonians invite strangers into their back gardens each summer
data.author: koolhead17
data.article_summary: 爱沙尼亚每年夏季都会举办"家庭咖啡馆日"活动，居民将自家花园、车库等私人空间临时改造成咖啡馆，向陌生人开放。这一传统始于2007年希乌马岛，旨在吸引游客。如今全国有150多场类似活动，时间集中在4月至9月。参与者提供自制食物和饮品，有的搭起帐篷，有的只是简单摊位。这个活动延续了爱沙尼亚社区互助(talgud)和好客的传统，让游客得以体验当地日常生活，同时展示各地区独特文化。活动既是社交盛事，也体现了邻里间的凝聚力。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：爱沙尼亚"家庭咖啡馆"（kodukohvikud）的真实性质——究竟是促进社交的邻里活动，还是包装过的商业行为

不同观点：

• **质疑派**（someoneeestis）：认为媒体描述误导，实际上这是付费商业活动，并非真正的社交邀请。爱沙尼亚人本身就不善于与陌生人交流，大多数顾客只是购买食物后独自用餐，90%的参与者没有特别的社交体验。

• **经济动机派**（Markoff）：直截了当指出这是为了赚钱（可能免税），与热情好客无关。

• **类比派**（Tomte、markvdb、tomaac_等）：提供其他欧洲国家的相似概念作为对比，如德国的临时酒庄餐厅、拉脱维亚的家庭咖啡馆、瑞典的二手货市场，暗示这是一种普遍的欧洲民间商业形式。

• **政治暗示派**（shevy-java）：暗讽爱沙尼亚人对俄罗斯人的态度，质疑其"开放性"的真实性。

补充讨论：多位评论者认同这是有趣的文化体验，但都对将其包装成"温暖的社交活动"持保留态度。核心争议在于：商业性质与社交意义之间的平衡点在哪里。

49163879.article_content:
Why Estonians invite strangers into their back gardens each summer
4 days ago
Share
Save
Add as preferred on Google
Hillary Millán
Martin Mark
Each summer, home gardens, garages and even bedroom windows across Estonia become temporary cafes open to anyone.
Beneath a giant tent, complete strangers queue to buy lunch. Around them, vegetable beds overflow with cucumbers, strawberries, garlic and courgettes, while an apple tree shades a table laden with rye bread, homemade pickles and a simmering pot of
seljanka
, a tomato-based soup with ham and smoked sausage. Guests order from a simple printed menu before carrying bowls of steaming soup to communal tables to eat.
At first glance, it looks like a country cafe. It isn't. It's Heiki Kalvik's back garden in the outskirts of Kehra, a small town about 45 minutes east of Tallinn, which he turns into a pop-up cafe each summer.
"I'm very outgoing, and I like to cook. I enjoy hosting, and I’m proud of our outdoor space," Kalvik says as another group of visitors arrives.
Kalvik is one of around a dozen residents taking part in Kehra’s annual Kodukohvikute Päev, or "home cafe day", when locals turn private gardens, courtyards and garages into temporary eateries for one day in July. Elsewhere in town, Karolin Vahtre has converted a garage behind her Soviet-era apartment block into a makeshift cafe, selling tempura sushi rolls, chanterelle quiche, chocolate cake and French fries to anyone who stops by.
Celine Senseney
Karolin Vahtre makes and serves tempura sushi rolls from her one-day garage café in Kehra (Credit: Celine Senseney)
More than 150
such events are held across Estonia between April and September, a beloved tradition that has spread steadily since the first event almost two decades ago. Some are elaborate, with rented tents, tables and chairs; others are little more than a lemonade stand manned by children. Together, they give visitors a rare glimpse of everyday Estonian life that is usually out of reach.
How to get involved
When to go:
Cafe days take place across Estonia from spring to early autumn, with many concentrated in July and August. Dates vary by town and region.
How to find one:
Check local tourism websites and search for 'Kohvikutepäevad' ("cafe days") on Facebook or in local event listings. Estonia's regional tourism sites also publish upcoming events.
What to expect:
These aren't conventional cafes or food festivals. Residents turn gardens, courtyards, garages, or other private spaces into temporary cafes, serving whatever they choose.
How Estonia's cafe days began
Estonia's home cafe tradition began on Hiiumaa, the country's second-largest island, in 2007 when local tourism promoters were looking for a way to attract visitors beyond the peak month of July.
They drew inspiration from Kärdla, the island's capital, and its long association with coffee. In the mid-1800s, the town was home to a broadcloth factory run by a Baltic German baron, who employed coffee-drinking workers from Central Europe. Local Estonians soon adopted the habit, with Kärdla residents eventually earning the nickname
kohvilähkrid
, or "coffee flasks", for taking coffee into the fields instead of the traditional sour milk or beer.
Fifteen homes took part in Hiiumaa's 2007 cafe days; today,
the three-day event
in early August attracts thousands of visitors, with dozens of temporary cafes selling homemade food and drinks across the island.
Hiiumaa Museum
is one of the few participants to have taken part every year since 2007, re-creating a 19th-Century cafe in its conference rooms at the Long House, the museum's main building and the former home of the broadcloth factory's managers. Its director, Kauri Kiivramees, says the tradition taps into something deeper than food and drink: the islanders' long history of welcoming outsiders.
Martin Mark
Menus vary from cafe to cafe, with some serving local specialties and others offering family favourites (Credit: Martin Mark)
Kiivramees says even this so-called "island of introverts" has always understood the importance of community: "It's quite traditional to help foreign visitors on Hiiumaa because back then it meant they were here because of [a] shipwreck or something like that, and they needed help."
From island tradition to national phenomenon
Small, rural communities have historically been the backbone of Estonian society on both the country's islands and mainland. While people aren't as reliant on their neighbours as they once were, certain traditions, like the
talgud
, have endured. These communal work days once involved haymaking or barn raising; today they are more commonly used for community clean-ups. Home cafe days reflect that same spirit of neighbourliness, and after their initial success on Hiiumaa, they soon spread across the country.
Setomaa in south-eastern Estonia, holds its
pop-up cafe days
every year on the second weekend in August, using the event to showcase its distinctive culture.

data.author: boplicity
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：新墨西哥州法院判决Meta支付5.67亿美元罚款，因其平台对未成年人心理健康造成损害

不同观点：

• **罚款实际很严重派**：从新墨西哥州人口比例看，罚款相当于Meta在该州5年总收入的一半到三分之二，是有史以来对科技公司最大比例的罚款之一，具有实际威慑力

• **罚款无效派**：多数评论认为这只是"商业成本"，Meta会无限期上诉拖延，最终支付金额会大幅减少或根本不会执行，相比全球收入仍是"零钱"

• **家长责任vs政府监管**：有人强调应由家长管控而非政府干预，担心去除网络匿名性弊大于利；但判决方认定平台造成公共妨害，损害公共健康和福利

• **产品成瘾性质疑**：有用户分享Instagram/TikTok如同"数字海洛因"的成瘾体验，删除后睡眠和心理状态明显改善

补充讨论：法律依据是新墨西哥州公共妨害法而非联邦CDA第230条豁免权；有人质疑社交媒体对儿童的价值；普遍对Meta会认真执行AI年龄预测等整改措施持怀疑态度

data.title: Obviously, DOGE Did Not Save Money
data.author: petethomas
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：美国政府"DOGE"项目的实际效果与真实目的

不同观点：

• **批评派（数据安全角度）**：认为DOGE未能节省资金，真实目的是泄露公民隐私信息，窃取数据并破坏调查，实际上已有GAO负责审计工作，DOGE是多余且危险的

• **批评派（人道主义角度）**：指出关闭USAID等项目导致全球范围内生命损失，且未经国会批准就切断援助，造成严重人道后果

• **温和派**：认可项目节约开支的初衷和精神，但认为执行过程缺乏谨慎指导，实践中效果不佳

• **支持派**：坚持DOGE确实节省了大量资金，认为GAO报告不可信（因为DOGE已关闭无法回应），强调DOGE要求说明开支用途的基本原则很有价值

补充讨论：有评论者注意到保守派旗舰媒体《国家评论》对此事的批评立场，认为这在政治上具有重要意义；另有人直接攻击支持者为"说谎者的狂热粉丝"，显示讨论已高度政治化和情绪化。争议焦点在于DOGE是否真正实现节约目标，还是以此为名实施政治破坏。

data.title: Spin audit of SQD/QSCI quantum-chemistry benchmarks on iron–sulfur clusters
data.author: purestatelabs
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：量子计算在材料模拟中的实际效用及其商业化问题

核心观点：
• **技术局限论**：当前有错误的量子计算机被当作量子系统的模拟器，但存在根本性障碍——真实材料中的电子是不可区分费米子，具有长程相互作用和量子关联，而flux qubit的自旋是可区分的且连接受限，模拟这些差异成本呈非线性增长，即使在简单案例中也无优势

• **长期无效论**：评论者指出这类研究已持续数十年（从其博士后时期至今），始终重复相同的主张和做法，但缺乏实际影响，认为稍有判断力的人都能看出问题

• **商业动机批判**：这类研究的真正驱动力是融资——能筹集比学术或软件开发岗位更多的资金，批评Google等公司也参与其中，将其比作"骗局"（fugazi）

• **建设性建议**：应继续投资量子计算硬件开发本身，但反对以牺牲科学真实性为代价来推广未成熟技术

补充讨论：评论者提到真实模拟还需考虑基组和相对论效应，使当前方案更加不切实际

data.title: An Agentic IDE That Builds Itself
data.author: sawyerjhood
data.article_summary:
bb 是一个开源的 AI 代理集成开发环境(IDE),最大特点是可以根据用户需求自我构建和扩展。与传统软件不同,每个用户的 bb 安装都可以完全不同——用户只需用自然语言描述需求,bb 就能为自己添加功能。

文章展示了多个定制案例:有人将其改造成任务管理系统、问题追踪界面、平铺窗口管理器、自动代码审查工具、Markdown 编辑器,甚至数字音频工作站。bb 采用 MIT 开源许可,支持 Codex、Claude Code、Cursor 等主流编码代理,用户使用自己的订阅即可。

核心理念是:现代软件成本降低,工具应该具备可塑性以适应个人工作流程,而不是强迫用户适应固定功能。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：AI驱动的可定制化IDE工具（bb）的优势与潜在问题

不同观点：
• **肯定派（willsr）**：实际使用体验良好，能够为特定领域（如硬件项目ECAD插件）构建完全可定制的工具，认为这种模式有广泛应用潜力，可扩展到GTM等其他领域

• **谨慎派（xg15）**：虽然认可工具的灵活性，但担忧"个性化软件时代"会导致重复造轮子问题——每个人都从零开始重建相同功能但实现方式不同，类似于JavaScript生态中库泛滥的困境。对于标准用例用户，"先提示再使用"的门槛可能过高

补充讨论：
xg15提出了建设性解决方案：建立扩展商店机制，允许用户分享和复用配置，通过扩展列表来标识特定配置。并指出LLM技术可以在识别恶意扩展和按功能分类扩展方面发挥作用，这可能缓解个性化带来的碎片化问题。

49203790.article_content:
← Blog
An Agentic IDE That Builds Itself
8/5/2026
I’m excited to show something I’ve been working on recently:
bb
, an agentic IDE that builds itself.
This started as a passion project by
@_ymichael
, and over time I changed from being an early user to a contributor.
bb
really worked for me in a way no other agent orchestrator has before and I think you’ll like it too.
Your first question is: ok, there are dozens of these, why this one?
"Did I cook??"
[picture of generic saas app sidebar]
— Brian Lovin (@brian_lovin)
August 3, 2026
No Two Installs Look Alike
Software of a previous generation looks something like this: there is a team somewhere who is solving a pain point for you. They might not solve it perfectly, but they are solving the problem for a set of people well enough and the economies of scale make it so that it is more efficient to buy their software vs building it yourself.
Software now is cheaper than ever before and I think those previous assumptions might no longer hold true. Software that you use needs to get the fundamentals right and be malleable enough to adapt to your use case.
This is where
bb
shines. It is a full agent orchestrator with solid fundamentals. It has a beautiful timeline and works with any coding agent using your own subscriptions. But the thing that sets it apart is that you can extend it in any way you see fit. Here is
bb
the first time you open it:
Threads on the left! I’ve never seen this before.
Here is my
bb
:
Yes, I’ve cloned Linear inside of my IDE.
Same install. Your imagination is the limit. Here is a set of things that people have added to
bb
all by just asking it to build it for them:
A task management system.
A full GUI for managing issues and agents automatically know how to read, create, and filter them.
A tiling thread management system.
A way to spatially navigate between all of your threads in two dimensions.
have been playing with doing tiling window management for agents conversations. it is a little too unhinged but i think there is something here.
pic.twitter.com/f9siynMwTd
— Sawyer Hood (@sawyerhood)
July 31, 2026
Automated code review.
A GitHub webhook that watches a repo for new PRs, pulls them, reviews them, and uses Codex computer use to test them end to end.
A markdown editor.
An Obsidian-like vault for markdown that you and your agents can edit. I’m writing this post in it right now.
A digital audio workstation.
I have a surface that lets me upload samples and prompt agents to create code using
Strudel
to do music production inside of
bb
.
Moreover, much of the functionality that ships with
bb
was built using the same extension system that you can use to have
bb
customize itself: provider agnostic workflows, the ask user question tool, side chat, crons, inline previews, and remote access are all plugins.
The Code Is Yours
bb
is an open source, MIT licensed agent orchestrator. It works with all of the popular coding agents out of the box (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, etc) and any agent that supports ACP, on your own subscriptions.
Clone it, run it, and then ask it for something it does not do yet.
I have not gone back to a tool I cannot change. I don’t think I will.

主要讨论点：关于允许单一所有者控制超过50%电视市场份额的监管政策

不同观点：
• **反对市场集中立场**：质疑允许单一所有者控制超过50%市场份额如何符合公共利益，担忧媒体垄断问题

• **电视已式微论**：认为本地电视台和传统电视已失去重要性，观众流失严重（主流新闻频道观众平均年龄60岁以上，20岁年轻人基本不看电视），因此市场集中度问题不再重要

• **支持整合观点**：认为行业整合可能是传统电视延缓完全崩溃的唯一途径，市场自然淘汰使监管变得不那么紧迫

• **程序性质疑**：关注监管委员会是否有权推翻国会裁决，认为权力制衡机制存在问题

补充讨论：有评论指出Brendan Carr（FCC主席）的能力问题，另有评论提示这是重复讨论话题。核心争议在于：在传统电视衰落的背景下，反垄断监管是否仍有必要。

data.title: Official: Ford's $29,945 Small EV Truck Is Called Fathom
data.author: thehoff
data.article_summary:
福特正式发布新款小型电动卡车Ford Fathom，起售价$29,945（约合人民币21.5万元），几乎与Maverick同价，但比F-150 Lightning便宜约2万美元。

Fathom基于福特全新通用电动平台打造，标准版搭载磷酸铁锂电池和后驱系统，另有大容量电池和四驱版本可选。车型采用四门配置，标准配备大尺寸触摸屏、Apple Maps导航、双向供电功能和BlueCruise自动驾驶技术。

福特通过大型铝铸件等制造创新大幅降低成本，CEO称这是"Model T时刻"，预示电动车革命性突破。新车预计2028年在肯塔基州投产。不过，"Fathom"这个名字引发了内部争议，公众反应有待观察。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：福特Fathom电动皮卡的结构设计、市场定位与技术特性

不同观点：

• **结构设计争议**：部分用户担忧结构电池设计的安全性（期待IIHS碰撞测试结果）和维修成本（电池老化后更换困难）；另一方则认可大型铝压铸工艺可能借鉴了比亚迪的先进技术，简化了100多个零件的集成

• **市场定位质疑**：有人质疑车辆命名（Fathom意为"英寻"应配6英尺货箱）和"小型"定位（实际尺寸接近Maverick并不算小）；但也有声音赞扬使用全新命名而非像Mustang Mach-E那样重用经典车名

• **动力系统偏好分化**：电动车支持者喜爱F-150 Lightning但期待更快充电（如中国的1MW充电）；传统燃油车用户强调Ranger的700公里续航和易维护性优势

• **技术配置分歧**：激进观点认为不支持自动驾驶的新电动车是"浪费钱"

补充讨论：争议核心在于集成化设计带来的制造效率与长期可维护性之间的权衡，以及电动化转型中不同用户群体对实用性、技术先进性的优先级差异。

49204344.article_content:
Official: Ford’s $29,945 Small EV Truck Is Called Fathom, Not Ranchero
The new pickup is almost the same price as Maverick—but is its name going to be a problem?
Alex Leanse
Writer
Aug 06, 2026
Save
Enough speculation has swirled about
Ford
’s forthcoming
small all-electric pickup truck
to fill the bed of an F-350 Super Duty. Today, the Blue Oval lightens that payload somewhat by officially announcing the new EV truck’s name and starting price, while confirming additional tech and capabilities.
0:00 / 0:00
This Goes Deep
“Ranchero” had been our guess at the truck’s title, but instead, an entirely new nameplate will be introduced. So here it is: Ford Fathom.
ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW
That aligns with the alliterative nomenclature Ford has used in the past with vehicles such as the Fusion, Focus, and Flex. There’s punny meaning behind the name, too. Ford said that in developing the truck it “reached a new depth of innovation, allowing the company to
fathom
possibilities once thought beyond reach.”
On learning the name, several
MotorTrend
staffers expressed their bewilderment with Ford’s choice, potentially portending a wider public reaction. But Fathom is official, and will designate what might be the most disruptive Ford since the F-150 Lightning.
ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW
Shallow Pockets? Here’s Your Truck
Perhaps any consternation around the name will fade when considering the starting price. The Fathom will begin at $29,945 ($28,350 plus a $1,595 destination fee).
That pricing is with the standard-range lithium-ion phosphate (LFP) battery, which is of an unknown size. Ford confirmed that it will offer a larger pack, extending driving range for extra cost. The entry-level Fathom will be rear-wheel drive, propelled by a permanent-magnet motor
designed and built by Ford
. An all-wheel-drive setup that adds an induction motor to the front axle will also be available.
ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW
This sub-$30,000 starting price demonstrates Ford’s obsession with
manufacturing efficiency
in developing the
Universal Electric Vehicle Platform
that underpins the Fathom and other future EVs. For example, the architecture uses
large aluminum unicastings
to incorporate more than 100 parts that would otherwise be separate, which simultaneously reduces the amount of fasteners used. Rather than a distinct floor component, the Fathom’s interior parts mount directly to the top of the structural battery.
For comparison, the Fathom’s $29,495 base price makes it roughly $20,000 less expensive than the cheapest versions of the F-150 Lightning in its
final year of production
. It’s barely more expensive than the
2026 Ford Maverick
, which starts at $29,685 for the XL trim with front-wheel drive and no options. A potential rival is the Slate Truck, which
starts at just $26,400
—but that might be a weaker value given the Fathom’s features.
ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW
ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW
Self-Driving Capable
Power windows will presumably be standard in the Fathom, which will be built in a four-door crew cab configuration. In that cab, Ford targets more passenger volume than a Toyota RAV4. The Fathom’s bed length is unknown but is probably similar to that of the Maverick, while an under-hood frunk will add additional capacity.
Ford said the Fathom's standard features will include a “large” infotainment touchscreen, built-in
Apple Maps navigation
, bidirectional power capability, and an app-based digital key. Every Fathom will be compatible with
BlueCruise
, Ford’s hands-free driving technology, which will likely be offered on a subscription basis.
Model T 2.0?
Ford’s EVs so far have been tepidly received. Although the
Mustang Mach-E
has sold decently, its name association with Ford’s beloved pony car may have been misguided. Despite massive investment in the F-150 Lightning, that pioneering electric pickup clashed with traditional truck values, and Ford, er, pulled the plug after 2025 while announcing it’ll re-engineer the Lightning to be a range-extender hybrid.
With this context, Ford is betting big on the Fathom and Universal Electric Vehicle Platform. Company CEO Jim Farley has called it a “Model T moment,” implying the revolutionary potential Ford sees in its forthcoming affordable EV models. The truck we now know as the Fathom will be the first of those when it rolls off the retooled line at
Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky
, likely for model year 2028.

data.title: Hackers Stalked Me by Hijacking a Smartwatch for Kids
data.author: worik
data.article_summary:
两位安全研究员在Black Hat会议上披露，超过70个品牌的GPS儿童智能手表和车载追踪设备存在严重安全漏洞。这些设备主要来自三个深圳供应链平台（YiQingTeng/Wonlex、NewGPS2012和SinoTrack），影响数千万设备。

研究员通过实际演示展示了漏洞的严重性：他们成功追踪WIRED记者的实时位置，秘密拍摄照片，窃听周围对话，而手表完全没有任何异常显示。这些漏洞源于缺乏基本的身份验证机制，黑客可以轻易访问任何设备，追踪儿童位置、篡改紧急联系人、伪造消息，甚至可能远程解锁或禁用车辆。

研究员警告称，这些低成本设备让数百万儿童面临被追踪和监控的风险，成为不法分子的"低垂果实"。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：儿童智能手表的安全漏洞及其背后的产品质量、监管和市场问题

不同观点：

• **质量标准批评派**：认为"深圳速度"和"快速行动"文化导致企业放弃工程标准，虽能短期获利但会侵蚀公众对产品的信任。这种持续的低级腐蚀可能比明显的安全缺陷造成更大的长期损害。

• **监管问题派**：指出中国政府未对这些不安全做法进行惩罚，中国制造商似乎不在乎出口产品的安全性，问题的根源在于缺乏有效监管。

• **消费者困境派**：强调市场上看似20种不同产品，实际可能都是同一设备连接同一个不安全后端。在这种情况下，"购买前做研究"的建议并不实用，消费者难以真正辨别。

• **替代方案推荐派**：建议购买Apple Watch SE等大品牌产品，强调其隐私保护、安全性和功能管控优势。

On a rainy
New York morning earlier this week, a WIRED reporter strapped to his wrist a lavender and pink plastic child’s
smartwatch
and headed to work. As he approached his nearby subway station to commute to WIRED’s office, he texted Vangelis Stykas, the Greek security researcher who had shipped him the watch via Amazon, to let him know that he was going into the station and might lose cell signal.
“I know,” Stykas wrote back.
In fact, Stykas had been monitoring the reporter’s location via the watch since the moment he left his apartment. The watch’s GPS feature, intended to let a parent track their child, was malfunctioning, but the wearable device was still picking up and transmitting to a faraway server identifiers from every nearby Wi-Fi network, which allowed Stykas to nonetheless pinpoint the reporter’s exact location as he walked down a particular Brooklyn block.
A WIRED reporter wearing the GPS-enabled smartwatch while holding an umbrella and walking to the subway earlier this week.
Courtesy of Andy Greenberg
When the reporter arrived at WIRED’s Manhattan headquarters half an hour later, Stykas hijacked a feature in the watch that allowed him to silently take a photo from its camera, capturing the moment when the reporter stepped into an elevator. After a few minutes, he took another snap of the reporter at his desk, then used a different feature to pick up audio from the watch’s microphone, transmitting it to another researcher, Felipe Solferini, who listened as the reporter’s coworker described his weekend visit to an art exhibition. At no point did the watch show any sign that it was listening, taking photos, or otherwise being hacked.
As WIRED reporter Andy Greenberg entered the elevator at WIRED's New York office, the hackers used the smartwatch to surreptitiously take a photo…
Courtesy of Vangelis Stykas
…and then again as he sat at his desk.
Courtesy of Vangelis Stykas
The watch’s insecurity and the spying it enabled might be expected given the gadget’s pedigree: It’s sold by an obscure company called CJC, costs less than $30, and was made by an equally obscure manufacturer, YiQingTeng Electronics, in Shenzhen, China. More troubling, perhaps, is that the online platform it’s built on—and the one that allowed Stykas and Solferini to so thoroughly hack it—is used by dozens of other brands of smartwatch, many of which have likely been left vulnerable to the same forms of digital stalking.
At the Black Hat cybersecurity conference today, Stykas and Solferini plan to present their findings from analyzing the supply chain and security of more than 70 GPS-enabled watches and car accessories. They found that more than 30 of those geolocation devices use the technology and backend servers of YiQingTeng, also identified by the brand name Wonlex, the name of a partner firm Shenzhen 3G Electronics, or their associated app, SETracker. Another 30-plus brands of tracking devices for cars and kids are all run on another Shenzhen-based platform known as NewGPS2012.
Combined with another major GPS platform known as SinoTrack that sells car trackers and smartwatches, the two researchers found that tens of millions of GPS tracker gadgets came from just three supply chains. All three, the researchers found in their analysis, had significant security flaws—in some cases as simple as a lack of authentication that allowed anyone to access any device—leaving children’s watches vulnerable to tracking by a hacker, location disabling and spoofing, interception and spoofing of text and audio messages sent to them, replacement of emergency contacts with ones a hacker chose, silent audio eavesdropping, as well as photo and video capture for camera-enabled devices. (Once the GPS started working on the smartwatch WIRED tested, the hackers showed that feature, too, could be hijacked to follow the wearer’s every move.)
For some GPS-enabled car accessories, the researchers found they could similarly track the devices’ locations or spoof messages to them that could potentially unlock or disable cars, though the researchers didn’t go so far as to test this out on actual vehicles. They also say they found server-side vulnerabilities that exposed consumer information, would have allowed them to execute their own code on the servers, or even in one case appeared to show that someone else had already gained unauthorized access to the system’s backend.
“Millions of kids are being exposed and vulnerable to exploitation. It's just catastrophic. It's really low-hanging fruit for a lot of bad actors,” Stykas says. “Your criminal mind is the only limitation in exploiting those devices.”
The Watches Watching Your Kids
The researchers say they’ve been warning the companies behind all three Shenzhen-based GPS platforms about their vulnerabilities for months. When WIRED reached a representative of SETracker, the person initially claimed in an email that “the

研究员通过实际演示展示了漏洞的严重性：他们成功追踪WIRED记者的实时位置，秘密拍摄照片，窃听周围对话，而手表完全没有任何异常显示。这些漏洞源于缺乏基本的身份验证机制，黑客可以轻易访问任何设备，追踪儿童位置、篡改紧急联系人、伪造消息，甚至可能远程解锁或禁用车辆。

Over the last decade, two of the most significant topics in defense research and development have been
directed energy systems
and
hypersonic weapons
. The Department of Defense and its major contractors have been pushing the boundaries of what is possible with these technologies and those efforts
could someday soon
literally
change the face of warfare
forever.
As it turns out, these two cutting edge areas of defense research are beginning to converge in laboratories with the goal of enabling unprecedented levels of speed for aerial weapons. By combining advanced directed energy technology with the latest in hypersonic vehicle design, researchers in private and Department of Defense (DoD) funded laboratories have laid the groundwork for systems designed to literally sheathe an entire vehicle in laser and/or microwave-induced plasma in order to drastically reduce drag. If successfully developed, this concept may someday lead to new frontiers in speed and radical new forms of aerodynamic control and aircraft design.
The Rapidly Evolving Hypersonic Landscape
As the world’s military superpowers jockey for position in a
new arms race
, hypersonic technologies have been pushed to the forefront of defense and aerospace research. These vehicles and weapons represent a true leap-ahead capability, enabling flight speeds that can outpace even the most advanced and robust air defense systems. It’s one thing to intercept and destroy a ballistic missile falling on an arcing path, but it’s another thing entirely to attempt to intercept a projectile moving at speeds greater than five times the speed of sound while executing abrupt changes in trajectory. It’s no surprise that hypersonic systems are becoming integral to the United States’ military’s future strategy in key theaters such as the Indo-Pacific region.
The need for hypersonic weapons has evolved alongside the parallel evolution of missile defense systems. As integrated sensor networks and missile defenses continue to become more sophisticated and adept, developing weapon delivery systems capable of evading or bypassing defenses with extreme speed has become paramount to ensuring global battlefield dominance and conventional deterrence. To that end, and
to keep
up
with foreign advances
, the USAF and other branches of the DoD have been
investing vast sums of money
into hypersonic research and development in recent years.
That R&D has already led to several systems approaching operational status. The USAF and Lockheed Martin are working on the AGM-183A
Air-launched Rapid Response Weapon
(ARRW), a boost-glide hypersonic system that is claimed to be able to
achieve speeds up to Mach 20
. The wedge-shaped ARRW has been tested in
captive flights on a B-52 Stratofortress
and is expected to be operational by 2022. Meanwhile, the Army and Navy, in conjunction with the Missile Defense Agency (MDA), have
tested their own hypersonic delivery system
, the Common Hypersonic Glide Body vehicle, or C-HGB. There are a number of other initiatives underway as well, including air-breathing hypersonic cruise missile designs,
such as HAWC
, and a multitude of classified efforts.
A Lockheed Martin-built AGM-183 ARRW (Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon) hypersonic missile during a captive flight test aboard a USAF B-52. ,
USAF
As with all hypersonic systems, drag and the resulting thermal stresses of extremely high-speed flight are two of the biggest hurdles faced by these vehicles. Even with advanced geometry, extreme levels of heat are generated by friction on the skin of high-speed craft, which can potentially degrade the structural integrity of the airframe and damage internal components, potentially even in a catastrophic fashion.
One of the ways of mitigating that heat buildup is to add shielding to the external surfaces of an airframe. That can increase a craft’s weight and may, therefore, decrease its range, maneuverability, and top speed. Thermal shielding requirements can also be very restrictive for aerospace designers that are looking to push the limits of inter-atmospheric speed.
Tweaking a vehicle’s geometry can mitigate drag, which can also help to reduce heat buildup. However, due to the limitations of materials science and the need to include various subsystems and payloads inside of hypersonic craft, there are restrictions on just how much the geometry can be altered. Thus, there is a pressing need for other drag reduction methods to be used in conjunction with airframe geometry. Like in many other areas of cutting-edge defense and aerospace research today, that’s where breakthroughs in directed energy may be able to lend a hand.

data.author: devonnull

新墨西哥州法院判决Meta公司因其平台对儿童心理健康造成伤害，需赔偿5.67亿美元。这是继今年3月里程碑式诉讼第一阶段判决后的第二阶段裁决。此前陪审团认定Meta故意伤害儿童心理健康并隐瞒平台上的儿童性剥削问题，罚款3.75亿美元。

赔偿金中4.2亿美元将用于青少年心理治疗服务，其余资金用于宣传预防、筛查服务等。法院还要求Meta改进平台功能，包括完善年龄验证、设置默认隐私保护、添加保护功能说明等。Meta发表声明表示不同意判决并将上诉，称公司一直努力保护平台用户安全。

New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567m over harms to children’s mental health
Ruling comes as part of second phase of landmark trial that found social media company enabled harm against users

A
New Mexico
court has ordered Meta, the parent company of Facebook, to pay $567m for mental health harm to children from its platforms.
Judge Bryan Biedscheid said the bulk of the money – $420m – would be used for treatment services for young people. The rest will go toward awareness and prevention, screening services and other costs over the next five years.
The ruling on Thursday comes as part of the second phase of a landmark trial the social media giant lost in March. At the time, a jury found that the company knowingly harmed children’s mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms, and
imposed a $375m fine
.
That trial
was the first to find
Meta liable for acts committed on its platform, and followed a Guardian investigation that revealed how Facebook and Instagram had become marketplaces for child sex trafficking.
In
the second phase
of the trial, prosecutors had asked the judge to impose fundamental changes at Meta aimed at reining in addictive features, improving age verification, and preventing child sexual exploitation through default privacy settings and closer oversight.
The judge has also ordered other changes, including that Facebook and
Instagram
build banner and informational screens to clearly explain its protection features, best practices, and tools to address inappropriate comment.
Those changes, and an educational campaign in New Mexico, would be subject to review by the state.
“We disagree with the ruling and will appeal,” said a statement issued by a
Meta
spokesperson late on Thursday.
“We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content. We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts,” it added.

data.title: New Orleans will use AI to answer 911 calls instead of a human
data.author: champagnepapi
data.article_summary: 新奥尔良正在测试AI系统接听911紧急电话,以减轻人工调度员负担。该市每天接到超过1000个紧急电话。AI主要用于分流同一事件的重复来电:当多人就同一事件报警时,AI会询问来电者是否与该事件相关,若是则提供信息更新,若不是则转接人工调度员。AI不直接处理真正的紧急情况,仅起到分类作用。但这种技术存在潜在风险,包括可能产生算法偏见、强化系统性种族歧视,以及难以识别口音较重或说话方式特殊的来电者,这可能影响紧急服务的公平性和可靠性。该系统需要严格的人工监督和数据训练才能有效运作。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：新奥尔良911呼叫中心使用AI处理紧急电话引发的争议

不同观点：

• **谨慎支持派**：认为在资源有限情况下，AI可以帮助分流高峰呼叫，官方数据显示处理效果良好（20个电话中正确处理15-18个，无误判）；对多语言、口音用户可能更友好；比长时间等待人工接听要好

49204546.article_content:
LOUISIANA
New Orleans will use AI to answer 911 calls instead of a human
Presley Bo Tyler
Shreveport Times
July 28, 2026, 6:02 a.m. CT
If you call 911 in New Orleans, you may hear the sound of an
artificial intelligence (AI)
agent answering your call instead of a human voice.
The Orleans Parish Communication District (OPCD) is changing the way dispatch calls are handled in New Orleans with the implementation of
new technology
.
The OPCD is currently testing out the
new tool
designed to reduce the volume of calls human dispatchers must handle, which is over a thousand emergency calls a day.
Why is New Orleans using AI to answer 911 dispatch calls? Here's how it works
New Orleans implemented AI in April to answer 311 calls for non-emergencies. The AI was trained and programmed to provide information to callers, as the OPCD says 50% of 311 calls are for information, according to
GovTech
.
How raw milk has caused 11 illnesses in Louisiana. What they contracted
Louisiana 'nuclear lifecycle' campus would handle disposal of nuclear waste
This Louisiana beach was named one of the best along the Gulf Coast
Is Congress banning weed drinks? New law goes into effect soon
3 Louisiana cities among the top 10 most dangerous places in the US
Louisiana suffering from near record-breaking heat. Will it get even hotter?
AI is now answering 911 emergency calls in Louisiana's largest city and one of the cities with the highest call rates in the U.S.
The OPCD is using Carbyne's AI Emergency Call Triage, with triage being the process of analyzing and prioritizing emergency calls. The AI system assesses incoming calls and can provide immediate feedback to callers.
This is intended to handle the increase of calls that are related to one incident, so callers get automatically routed to an AI agent who asks if they are calling regarding the incident. If the answer is yes, then callers can receive information or updates, and if it's no, then the callers are transferred to a human.
This combats multitudes of calls piling up and taking longer time to potentially answer an emergency call. The OPCD said the AI will not be used to handle emergency calls, only to direct such calls to a human dispatcher.
Potential negative impacts of using AI to answer 911 calls instead of a human
While AI can help with 911 response times and dispatch efficiency, there are risks in relying on an AI bot to successfully handle all emergency calls.
AI-powered 911 triage is programmed to divert non-urgent calls during surges in the number of calls. By dispatchers identifying repeated patterns, like influxes of calls during rush hour traffic reporting accidents, the data is used to train AI to predict such patterns and handle calls related to the same incident.
With human oversight, thorough training data, strong cybersecurity and algorithm regulation, AI 911 triage can work effectively, but AI can be unreliable if not properly monitored and outcomes sometimes aren't guaranteed.
For instance, it's possible AI could develop hidden biases. If AI is used for predictive policing algorithms, generating an analysis for when and where crime are most likely to occur, it's possible for results to be skewed by historical crime data from over-policed neighborhoods and marginalized communities. Based on this, the AI would essentially reinforce systemic racism and socioeconomic bias, according to
Police1
.
It's also possible that AI agents handling 911 triage could fail to understand individuals with stronger accents and dialects, as well as differences in pitch and articulation. This is because AI is programmed with automatic speech recognition systems and, therefore, could potentialy be unreliable when presented with a speech unlike the ones used the AI is trained to recognize.
Presley Bo Tyler is the Louisiana Deep South Connect Team reporter for USA Today Network. Find her on X @PresleyTyler02 and email at PTyler@Gannett.com

of missiles.
After five months of war with Iran, stockpiles of long-range weapons are so low, current and former U.S. defense officials told us, that they don’t believe the U.S. has enough to combat a threat in Asia. The remaining supplies, depending on the munition, are as low as 20 percent of what the Pentagon would like to have in hand. And stores of sophisticated interceptor missiles, such as Patriots and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missiles, are too depleted to give or sell the weapons to Ukraine or effectively defend against Iran’s launch of ballistic missiles. Even when troops see Iranian missiles approaching, they are forced to decide in a matter of seconds whether to expend a limited number of interceptors or hope for the best, the defense officials told us.
Defense Secretary
Pete Hegseth
this week pleaded with Republicans on Capitol Hill for billions of dollars to replenish America’s dangerously depleted stockpiles of missiles and other crucial munitions. Hegseth’s appeal was nakedly partisan—he ignored Democratic lawmakers entirely—but also long overdue.
The Pentagon this year has awarded tens of billions of dollars in contracts to replenish those arsenals. But signing contracts is not the same as delivering missiles. Those contracts will produce munitions over the coming years, not the coming months. The Trump administration has invested in the defense industrial base to accelerate production, as did the Biden administration, but for crucial systems such as the Patriot, supply is not projected to meet demand until about 2030. Meanwhile, Iran has ramped up production of its offensive drones and ballistic missiles, and enhanced their capabilities. The war is now being shaped as much by industrial supply and logistics as by economic considerations and the politics of the midterms.
P
resident Trump raged
at the assessment his national-security team gave him at Camp David on Friday, which showed that the U.S. military was running low on the munitions that would be necessary for Trump to order an escalation against Iran, a senior administration official familiar with the meeting told us. If the U.S. were to strike, Tehran would likely launch a barrage of missiles and drones against its neighbors in the region and the American bases they host.
The president barked at aides and had some pointed words for the Department of Defense’s leadership. (He is not presently considering staff changes, a White House official told us.) Trump has grown frustrated at his inability to escape the stalemate of the war; he’s seething at its toll on the economy and is desperate to move on. In a post on Truth Social earlier today, Trump said that reports of munitions shortages were false and that such “leaks” were treasonous. Manufacturers are shipping “large amounts” of munitions “as needed,” he wrote.
Read: This may be Trump’s biggest error in the Iran war
White House aides are concerned that Trump is losing his leverage in the conflict. He has threatened Iran many times but has rarely followed through; Tehran knows that. Tehran also knows that the U.S. is running low on munitions despite what Hegseth and the president say in public. Military leverage depends not simply on the U.S. ability to strike but also on its capacity to defend against Iran’s retaliation. Iran has displayed the confidence to further test the U.S., attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz. The White House has maintained that Iran would soon face an economic situation so dire that the regime would be forced to negotiate, and U.S. intelligence reports suggest that Iran is struggling. But the Trump administration has been surprised at Tehran’s resilience, and is no longer certain that the regime will reach the point where negotiation is its only option.
In the five months since the war started, the president has never faced such a weak position. The shortage of interceptors makes escalation dangerous. Nor would expanded strikes guarantee that Tehran will come back to the table.
That may leave diplomacy and concessions as the administration’s least risky option. Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have repeatedly said that Iran will never be allowed to control any part of the Strait of Hormuz. The proposed agreement between Oman and Iran, pending U.S. and Gulf approval, would reopen the strait by establishing a jointly managed framework for commercial shipping. Trump again tries to limit US birthright citizenship with new executive orders
1 hour ago
Share
Save
Add as preferred on Google
Grace Eliza Goodwin
Watch: Trump signs executive orders targeting birthright citizenship
Donald Trump is trying again to scale back birthright citizenship in the US, weeks after the Supreme Court shot down his previous attempt to eliminate the right.
The president signed two executive orders on Thursday, including one that expands the existing definitions of non-citizens whose children are not eligible for birthright citizenship.
The second order bans so-called birth tourism, the practice of pregnant mothers coming to the US to give birth so that their babies will be citizens.
"This should have happened years ago, but we're taking care of it now," Trump said from the Oval Office, criticising the Supreme Court's rejection of his previous bid to end the 150-year-old policy.
"My Administration has guarded against the risks posed by malign foreign actors who attempt to swindle American citizens by taking advantage of the generosity of our Nation," the first executive order says.
That order prohibits the automatic citizenship of babies born in the United States to two non-citizen parents where one of the parents is: a member of a foreign terrorist group, a foreign government employee, has attempted to gain citizenship through fraudulent means, or is living in US territories where citizenship is not conferred by federal statute.
Birthright citizenship for people born in US territories such as Puerto Rico is codified by federal statute.
Trump and members of his administration have repeatedly railed against birth tourism, including accusing Russian and Chinese adversaries of taking advantage of birthright citizenship to infiltrate the US.
While announcing the executive orders from the Oval Office on Thursday, Trump said that hundreds of thousands of babies have been born through birth tourism in the US.
Bloomberg via Getty Images
The Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan research group, has said that the most expansive census-based estimate accounts for about 22,000 to 26,000 babies born in the US from birth tourism every year. Government data, according to the institute, showed that there were 9,600 births to mothers with foreign addresses in 2024.
"The idea (is) that people come here pretending to be a tourist, pretending to be a visitor," Stephen Miller, homeland security advisor and White House deputy chief of staff for policy, said while standing beside the president on Thursday.
"But the real reason they're here is to have a child, to make that child an automatic citizen, (to) leave our country and then have a US citizen child," he said, adding that thoe children then gain access to welfare benefits, the voting booth, and "all the other rights and privileges that belong solely to Americans".
Miller said the president has the authority to ban birth tourism under a section of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which grants the president the power to set exceptions and limitations on who can enter into the country.
On one of his first back days in office in 2025, Trump signed an executive order that tried to end birthright citizenship as guaranteed in the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution.
A legal battle brought the case to the Supreme Court, which in June ruled that Trump's 2025 policies could not stand and birthright citizenship remained the law.
The decision was a major blow to Trump's ongoing efforts to limit who can live, work, and become citizens in the US.
The high court made "a bad decision, very unfair decision", Trump said from the Oval Office on Thursday while announcing the executive orders. "Our country suffers because of it, and we're ending in a different way."
Gabriel Chin, a professor at the University of California Davis' School of Law, told the BBC that while parts of the order might hold up, other aspects "raise some serious constitutional questions".
Chin said the president does have some power to restrict people coming into the US specifically for the purposes of having a child.
"But once it does happen, once a child is born in the United States, I don't think the president has any power to decide that that child is not a citizen," he said, adding that the issue was settled in the Trump administration's recent loss in the Supreme Court.
He called birth tourism a "drop in the bucket" against the millions of births in the US.
"It's an unusual phenomenon," he said.

data.title: São Paulo resident transforms degraded area into urban forest
data.author: rmason
data.article_summary:
2003年，退休人士Helio da Silva开始在圣保罗一片废弃土地上独自种树。他用个人积蓄（每年约7000美元）坚持耕耘，许多人认为这是不可能完成的任务。

20年后，这片曾经荒芜的土地已转变为该市最大的城市森林之一。2008年，该地被正式认定为圣保罗首个线性公园——Tiquatira公园，全长约3.2公里，拥有数千棵树木和约160个物种，吸引了数十种鸟类栖息。

如今73岁的da Silva虽已退休，但仍每天巡视公园，修剪照料树木。他用一个人的坚持，为拥有1200万人口的圣保罗创造了一片宝贵的绿色空间，展示了个人行动如何改变城市环境。

2003年，退休人士Helio da Silva开始在圣保罗一片废弃土地上独自种树。他用个人积蓄（每年约7000美元）坚持耕耘，许多人认为这是不可能完成的任务。

20年后，这片曾经荒芜的土地已转变为该市最大的城市森林之一。2008年，该地被正式认定为圣保罗首个线性公园——Tiquatira公园，全长约3.2公里，拥有数千棵树木和约160个物种，吸引了数十种鸟类栖息。

如今73岁的da Silva虽已退休，但仍每天巡视公园，修剪照料树木。他用一个人的坚持，为拥有1200万人口的圣保罗创造了一片宝贵的绿色空间，展示了个人行动如何改变城市环境。

data.article_summary: 这篇文章讲述了芝加哥大学校友Faber Birren (EX'23) 的传奇故事。他是20世纪色彩理论与应用的先驱人物。Birren出生于艺术世家，曾就读芝加哥大学，后辍学专注自学色彩研究。1930年代起，他开始向工业界推广色彩设计理念，通过科学实验证明色彩对消费者心理和工作效率的影响。他为肉类公司、工厂、医院等设计色彩方案，帮助提升销售和改善工作环境。1945年出版的《用色彩销售》一书奠定了他的权威地位。他的工作将色彩从艺术领域带入商业和工业应用，被《纽约时报》誉为"最权威的色彩专家"，深刻影响了现代色彩设计和大众心理学研究。

“The story of color is almost the story of civilization itself,” Birren wrote in 1963. (Illustration by Cheryl Chalmers)
Shades of meaning
Twenty-nine years after his death, the work of Faber Birren, EX’23, still colors the world around us.
By
Author
Christopher Good, ’19
|
The University of Chicago Magazine
—
Spring/18
“I am convinced when I say that color has been a neglected art,” Faber Birren, EX’23, declared in 1934.
No one could make the same claim today, eight decades on. Certain slivers of ROYGBIV—like Tiffany blue or T-Mobile magenta—have been copyrighted under federal law, while others have inspired scientific inquiry and even public policy interventions. Take Baker-Miller pink, a shade some believe has a soothing effect (the experimental evidence for this claim is mixed). Endorsers include supermodel Kendall Jenner, who painted her living room in the bubblegum-like hue, and prison officials in Switzerland, where every fifth prison or police station has at least one pink cell.
How color came to a place of such cultural and commercial prominence is a big question, but it has some answers in the life and writings of Birren, an unconventional consultant and theorist who proclaimed that he was concerned with color “not as individual feeling and expression but as mass psychology and mass reaction.” Over a nearly 60-year career, Birren went from a self-taught enthusiast to “the most authoritative source” on color according to the
New York Times
.
Birren didn’t just demystify his subject: he “put color to work,” as he described it, in 20th-century America, from the machinery of heavy industry to the linoleum of suburban kitchens. Alongside these commercial efforts, he wrote probing reflections on more speculative, less understood aspects of color—its power to heal us and to change how we feel.
After emigrating from Luxembourg, Birren’s grandfather Henry Birren settled in Chicago in 1848 and became an undertaker. Faber wrote in a 1928 family history that it was “out of pure love for beauty, in spite of his heritage of frugality” that he drove “the finest hearse that graced the city’s streets.”
Joseph Birren—Henry’s youngest son, and the only one not to become an undertaker—started as a professional painter in 1885, when he was recruited to work on a 360-degree picture, or cyclorama, of the Battle of Gettysburg. (“He was the only painter on the staff who could achieve the task of making a dead soldier look dead,” Faber wrote.) Joseph traveled the world, drew illustrations for newspapers, and earned acclaim for a 1924 solo exhibition at the Art Institute of Chicago.
That Faber is an anagram of the German
Farbe
, for color, seems to be a coincidence—Faber shared his given name with his grandmother Catherine’s maiden name. Still, it fit. As a child, he drew on walls and painted murals; as a teen, he experimented with dyes.
After a brief stint at the Art Institute, Birren arrived at the University of Chicago in the fall of 1919 with plans to study education. He discovered he didn’t miss making art but couldn’t shake his interest in studying color—and such a program didn’t exist at the University of Chicago, or any other academic institution. In the spring of 1921, Birren dropped out, committed to educate himself about color, and became a regular at the Chicago Public Library.
Birren’s early studies were, in a word, eccentric. At one point he resolved to test an old scrap of folklore—that being surrounded by red walls could make a person go mad—by coating his entire bedroom with vermillion paint. In a week’s time, the only change he could gather was that he felt cozy and cheerful.
In 1935 Birren left Chicago for New York City, where he began to evangelize about color design to skeptical industrialists. He promised a Chicago wholesale meat company he could boost their sales—the white walls of the company’s coolers, he believed, lent the meat an unappealing gray tinge. Birren studied porterhouse steaks under various lights before determining a blue-green backdrop would make the beef look redder. Sales went up, and before long the company’s top competitor changed its color scheme too.
Faber Birren “put color to work,” from the machinery of heavy industry to the linoleum of suburban kitchens. (Infographic by Chloe Reibold)
It wasn’t until color was found to have an impact on bottom lines that Birren gained a real audience with corporate America. In 1945’s
Selling with Color
(McGraw-Hill), Birren related stories from his own clients (painting office walls a darker tone than machinery reduced irritability and inattentiveness among workers, he found); best practices (in hospitals, operating rooms should be blue-green, while private patient rooms should be decorated in warm, light tones); and, for good measure, a smattering of interesting stories he’d heard (Purdue University, he learned, developed red nail polish for agricultural laborers to compare against the ripeness of tomatoes).

data.author: divyenduz
data.article_summary: 这篇文章记录了作者学习FPV（第一人称视角）无人机飞行的经历。作者先在Liftoff模拟器中练习了约20小时，掌握基本操控后决定尝试真实飞行。他购买了新手友好的BetaFPV Air65微型无人机（17克）、Fat Shark Echo护目镜、充电器和电池等装备，并利用AI助手帮助选购和比价。文章指出真实飞行比模拟器困难得多，需要理解大量专业术语，完成设备绑定、频道调试、电池管理等配置工作。作者强调微型无人机适合新手入门，因为它们耐摔、安全且相对便宜。整体而言，这是一篇面向FPV无人机初学者的经验分享。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：关于使用AI辅助学习和构建FPV无人机/飞行器的必要性和方法

不同观点：

• **反对使用AI辅助的传统主义观点**（yial）：认为不需要AI来学习FPV技术，应该专注理解硬件工作原理（发射器、接收器、电源系统、螺旋桨、电机等）。强调现代设备已经很容易上手（即插即用、无需手动PID调参），通过社区连接和实践飞行（特别是视距飞行）来学习更有价值。建议关注乐趣本身而非过度依赖技术辅助。

• **对AI学习方式的质疑**（spaqin）：指出网上已有大量免费知识和活跃社区，使用LLM询问问题没有额外价值，反而失去了社区互动的意义。社区成员习惯重复回答相同问题，这种人际互动是学习过程的重要部分。

• **对内容的安全担忧**（bjelkeman-again）：从完全不同角度提出担忧，认为展示的视频内容看起来像军事训练（如乌克兰战场的无人机作战），对技术应用的伦理问题表示不安。

• **支持态度**（iamanllm）：简单表达了对分享内容的感谢和认可。

补充讨论：核心争议在于学习方式的选择——是依赖AI快速获取信息，还是通过传统的社区互动和动手实践深入理解？同时出现了对技术应用场景的伦理关切，但这一点未得到其他人回应。

49161803.article_content:
Learning to fly FPV drones with AI flight coach
Divyendu Singh
Aug 03, 2026
Share
I recently got into flying FPV drones and wanted to share my learning experience. Learning anything is understanding terminology, repetition and loads of practice. I aim currently at a place where I can be air borne for 30 seconds to 1 minute or so on a real tiny whoop drone. That means I am at the beginning of my learning journey and have used the word “learning” very generously.
This post is also not a 101 to get into flying FPV drone, however, I have linked enough posts for you to get going, if you read this post and all the linked links.
Divyendu’s Notes is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Subscribe
The beginning: simulators
I actually don’t remember how I got into it but about a year or so ago I purchased a RadioMaster Pocket radio / controller and started flying a bit in Liftoff simulator. I was following the
famous playlist from Joshua Bardwell
. I highly recommend that as a starting point.
I think my source was running into the
Flow State documentary
on YouTube but I am not sure.
Anyways, after about 10 hours practice in Liftoff this hobby died for the moment and I wouldn’t get to it until a year or so later.
I got back to the Liftoff simulator (early July 2026) and after another 10 hours of flying (20 simulator hours total), I felt I was no longer useless in the simulator i.e. I could recover from going out of bounds which was very hard before and crash less when trying things, kinda maintain my altitude and overall started enjoying it as a game.
Liftoff has a mode called “slipstreams” in which you can chase a car with drone thereby simulating making a cinematic car chase video. I started playing it like a game and really enjoyed it (albeit it was and still is pretty hard).
Here is a video of me in simulator after 20-30 hours of flying practice (maybe less?)
Let’s try it for real
At this point, I thought I was ready to try some real life drone flying and for that I explored the excellent OscarLiang blog
https://oscarliang.com/fpv-drone-guide/
Based on this guide, I knew that I have to start with a tiny whoop (<30g drones) for several reasons.
They can take a lot of beating / crashes and therefore are perfect for newbies like me.
They are small and have less licensing / formal requirements. TL;DR they are just safer.
FPV done flying seems like a pretty expensive hobby and they are relatively cheap to get into the hobby
The minimum set of gear you need to be air borne is (and listing what I got and why)
Drone - I got an BetaFPV Air65, it is a very tiny 17g drone that can take a lot of beating and highly recommended for beginners.
FPV Goggles - I got Fat Shark Echo. They are not the cheapest available goggles but if I keep into this hobby and want to fly outdoors, I can keep using them. It also has a recording feature.
LiPo Battery Charger - I got a ViFly Whopstor 3. It can charge the batteries safely and also has a storage feature. LiPo batteries when not to be used must be at middle point of their voltage for longevity.
LiPo batteries - I got Betafpv lava 320mAh. They were recommended for my requirements by both OscarLiang blog and AI agent.
New toys - Air 65, Fat Shark Echo
Purchasing the gear was the first instance where I used AI seriously. While I had a good idea of roughly what I wanted from reading the OscarLiang blog. I made AI agent
agy
(Google antigravity) look up available gear, compare prices in local shops across EU and actually override some decisions like getting a Fat Shark Echo vs a totally entry level FPV goggles.
Reality is unforgiving
Simulator was easy. As far as I remember, the day RadioMaster pocket arrived, I didn’t have to do anything really except calibration in Liftoff to be air borne in a simulator. But getting the real gear to talk to each other requires work and understanding a lot of terminology. The FPV world is vast and has many jargon terms (most annoying part of learning anything new for me). OscarLiang has a nice
glossary blog page
, which got me going.
But very roughly here is what you need at the very least to get going
Bind your drone to the radio master pocket radio.
This is what I followed
:
plug replug the battery from drone 3 times
in RadioMaster pocket, press sys, scroll to bind, click bind
if bound, pressing the arm button (LB in PlayStation speak) should Arm the drone i.e. the propellors start moving
Tune Fat Shark Echo to the broadcast frequency. The FPV video goggles don’t “bind” to get the video feed. The drone broadcasts the video feed at 5.8 GHz and the Fat Shark Echo receives the feed. You need to tune the channel and luckily it has a button on top that auto scans for the channel. When in sync, your goggles should show something like this
Charge the batteries, in my case to 4.85V for flying and 3.85 for storage. Do not go below 3.3V for long, that can damage the batteries permanently

data.article_summary: Ruby 包管理器 Bundler 4.0.18 版本扩展了供应链安全控制机制。该版本将"冷却期"(cooldown)功能扩展到 `bundle lock` 和 `bundle cache` 命令,这意味着在生成�file文件和进行 gem 依赖包本地化(vendoring)时,系统会延迟使用刚刚发布的新 gem 包。这一安全措施旨在通过延迟采用新发布的依赖包,降低 Ruby 项目遭受供应链攻击的风险。

data.title: What are Looped Transformers? Explained clearly
data.author: gmays
data.article_summary:
Looped Transformers（循环Transformer）是一种提升AI智能的新方法：不是增加参数或训练数据，而是让输入在同一层权重中循环处理多次，就像反复阅读来加深理解。例如，训练25层但循环4次，可获得100层的效果，参数量却减少4倍。

这个想法源于2018年的Universal Transformers论文，但当时未能流行，因为正值"规模至上"时代，且基础设施不成熟。现代版本结合了Mixture of Experts、稀疏注意力等新技术，在推理任务和抽象问题求解上表现出色。核心优势是让相同权重具备多态性——能够反思和迭代自身输出，在保持计算量的同时大幅减少存储的权重数量。

What are Looped Transformers? Explained clearly
So there are basically two ways people make a LLM "smarter":
1. give it more parameters (a bigger brain),
2. or, give it more compute/data to train on (a longer education).
Both work, but both are expensive!
The ultimate motive of all types of research is to maximize objectives under resource constraints. In that light, we would rather be chasing a tempting third option: reuse the parameters you already have, instead of buying new ones.
The idea has led the world to discover/invent a Looped Transformer.
A looped transformer takes a section of the model and run the same input through it multiple times in a loop, letting it "think" a bit more each pass, almost like re-reading a paragraph a few times to understand it better. If this works, you could get the intelligence benefits of a much bigger model while only storing the weights of a small one.
Instead of training 100 transformer layers, you might train 25 layers, but loop over them 4 times.
The forward pass latency and the number of FLOPs remain similar, but the number of weights decrease 4x.
Effectively, you have trained your weights to be polymorphic - the same weights are capable of reflecting and iterating over past versions of its own output.
Looped models have done surprisingly well on reasoning-heavy tasks, in-context learning, and abstract puzzle-solving benchmarks like ARC-AGI and Sudoku.
The earliest Looped Transformer
One of the most cited papers is this little known 2018 ICLR paper on "Universal Transformers"
In Universal Transformers we take the standard Transformer and replace its fixed stack of N distinct layers with a single shared transition function applied recurrently across time steps.
Instead of processing depth as "layer 1 → layer 2 → ... → layer N," UT iteratively refines the representation of every position in parallel, applying the same weights at each recurrent step.
Some of these themes are present in classic RNNs (recurrent neural networks) as well, where a single module is reused multiple times to process data sequentially. Whereas RNNs looped over the entries in a sequence across time, UT (and Looped Transformers as well) processes each input token parallelly across time. The loop is only applied at the layer level.
UT got a lot of cool results but its lasting legacy is for introducing this crazy idea. It is now cited as the direct architectural ancestor of essentially every modern looped/recurrent-depth language model.
Why UT "failed" (in 2018)
There are several reasons why UT wasnt perceived as a bigger deal back then.
1. The compute-vs-parameters trade-off wasn't understood yet
Given an N× increase in compute, simply making the model N× bigger tends to beat looping it N times. In 2018-19, scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020) hadn't even been published, so the field had no formal framework for asking "is recurrent compute or parameter compute more valuable per FLOP?" UT was evaluated at matched parameter count, not matched training compute, which flatters recurrence (recurrent steps are "free" parameters) while hiding its true compute cost.
2. The timing was wrong
UT (2018) landed right as the field was entering the "scale is all you need" era. Think of all the work that came back then: BERT (2018), GPT-2 (2019), and soon GPT-3 (2020) demonstrated that brute-force parameter and data scaling of vanilla, easily-parallelizable Transformers delivered massive, predictable gains. Recurrent depth is fundamentally sequential - you cannot compute step t+1 until step t finishes. 3. Infrastructure wasn't ready
3. The gains were real but not dramatic enough
UT was more of a research paper than a full blown millions of dollars model. The results were cool but they did not feel huge enough to shift the paradigm back then, because the scale they operated in was small.
4. Advances in tech
UT was tested only as a dense architecture. Modern LTs work with knowledge of 7 more years of dedicated research and funds. We got Mixture of Experts models now, more advanced sparse attention methods (like DSA, and more recently CSA).
UT was also an encoder-decoder architecture. In current times, all LMs are decoder only architectures.
5. Compute money
GPUs in 2026 are way more capable than in 2019. Investors are also more likely to invest in cutting edge AI research right now than back in 2019 (which is kinda surprising given most of the backbone of modern AI was arguably built from 2017-2020).
The Modern Looped Transformer (Latent Thinking)
Universal Transformer's core idea was: apply the same self-attention + transition block repeatedly, refining the representation of every token in parallel, with per-token halting deciding when each symbol is "done."
The modern Looped Transformer keeps the same weight-tying thing alive but reframes almost everything else around what a decoder-only, billion-to-trillion-parameter causal language model needs: efficient training at scal

data.title: The DISTINCT in Your COUNT
data.author: gmcabrita
data.article_summary:
这篇文章分析了 PostgreSQL 中 `count(DISTINCT)` 查询无法并行执行的问题。

文章对比了两个查询:普通的 `count(*)` 可以利用多个并行 worker 分片扫描并合并结果,而 `count(DISTINCT user_id)` 却退化为单核串行执行,甚至需要将数据溢出到磁盘。

根本原因在于 DISTINCT 聚合的特性:它必须在一个地方看到所有值才能去重。并行聚合依赖于各 worker 的部分状态可以合并,但不同 worker 的 distinct count 无法简单相加——因为同一用户可能出现在多个 worker 的数据分片中。要正确合并就必须传输完整的去重集合,这违背了并行化的初衷。因此查询规划器无法为 DISTINCT 聚合生成并行计划,导致性能显著下降。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：数据库 COUNT(DISTINCT) 性能优化方法，以及对 AI 生成技术文章的质量担忧

不同观点：
• **技术质疑派**：认为原文关于 COUNT(DISTINCT) 不能并行化的论点存在问题，实际上可以通过 COUNT(*) GROUP BY 实现并行计数，怀疑文章缺乏深入理解

• **技术补充派**：建议使用概率算法（如 Flajolet-Martin、HyperLogLog）来近似计算 DISTINCT 值，这些方法只需 10 行代码且无需排序，适合对精确度要求不高的场景

• **内容质量批判派**：对 AI 生成的技术文章持消极态度，认为即使内容不算完全"垃圾"，也难以激发有价值的技术讨论

补充讨论：评论者们普遍关注技术文章的真实性和深度。当技术论述出现逻辑漏洞时，容易引发对文章是否由 LLM 生成的怀疑，这反映了技术社区对 AI 生成内容可信度的担忧。

Table of Contents
The schema
Two counts, two different plans
Why the planner can't split it
One DISTINCT poisons the whole statement
The rewrite: push the DISTINCT into a GROUP BY
ORDER BY aggregates hit the same wall
The harder case: per-group distinct counts
When to actually care
Here is a query that shows up in every analytics workload:
SELECT
count
(
DISTINCT
user_id)
FROM
events;
It looks like the cheapest possible thing: count the distinct users. On a machine with cores to spare you would expect Postgres to throw a few parallel workers at it and be done. It does not. That one keyword,
DISTINCT
, switches off parallel query for the entire statement, and the larger your table the more it costs you. And to make it even worse there's no setting or index changes that. The problem is in a way how aggregate has to execute.
The schema
Ten million events, about fifty thousand distinct users, a handful of countries. Nothing unusual.
CREATE TABLE
events
(
id
bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
,
user_id
int    NOT NULL
,
country
text   NOT NULL
,
amount
numeric
(
10
,
2
)
NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO
events (user_id, country, amount)
SELECT
(random()
*
50000
)::
int +
1
,
(
ARRAY
['US','DE','GB','FR','JP','BR','IN','CA'])[(random()*7)::int + 1],
(random()
*
500
)::
numeric
(
10
,
2
)
FROM
generate_series
(
1
,
10000000
);
ANALYZE events;
max_parallel_workers_per_gather
is at its default of 2 on fresh cluster. For these examples I raised it to 4 and
work_mem
to 64MB, so there's no resource starvation to blame for the plans below.
Two counts, two different plans
Start with a plain
count(*)
, which has nothing to deduplicate:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS
OFF
)
SELECT
count
(
*
)
FROM
events;
Finalize Aggregate (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
->  Gather (actual rows=5.00 loops=1)
Workers Planned: 4
Workers Launched: 4
->  Partial Aggregate (actual rows=1.00 loops=5)
->  Parallel Seq Scan on events (actual rows=2000000.00 loops=5)
Four workers plus the leader (
loops=5
) each scan their slice and keep a running count, and the leader adds the five partial counts together at the end.
Now add one word:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS
OFF
, BUFFERS)
SELECT
count
(
DISTINCT
user_id)
FROM
events;
Aggregate (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
Buffers: shared hit=15915 read=47783, temp read=14681 written=14684
->  Sort (actual rows=10000000.00 loops=1)
Sort Key: user_id
Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 117448kB
Buffers: shared hit=15915 read=47783, temp read=14681 written=14684
->  Seq Scan on events (actual rows=10000000.00 loops=1)
Buffers: shared hit=15912 read=47783
No
Gather
. No
Partial Aggregate
. No parallel scan. A single process reads all ten million rows, sorts every one of them by
user_id
so duplicates sit next to each other, then walks the sorted output counting the runs. The sort does not fit in 64MB of
work_mem
, so it spills 115MB to a temporary file on disk. One core, the whole table, plus disk IO that the parallel
count(*)
never touched.
Why the planner can't split it
The sort is how Postgres computes
DISTINCT
inside an aggregate: order the values and adjacent equal ones collapse. A hash table is the other option, but the classic
DISTINCT
-aggregate path sorts. Either way it has to see every value in one place, which is the whole problem.
Parallel aggregation in Postgres works in two halves. Each worker runs a
Partial Aggregate
that builds
transition state
, a small running summary of the rows it has seen. For
count
that state is just a number. The leader then runs a
Finalize Aggregate
that merges those partial states with the aggregate's
combine function
, the thing that knows how to fold two partial states into one.
count
's combine function adds the partial counts.
sum
,
avg
,
min
,
max
all have one. This split, scan in parallel, combine at the end, is the entire basis of parallel query for aggregates.
count(DISTINCT user_id)
has no usable combine step, and not because nobody wrote one. Think about what a worker could hand back. To merge two workers' results into a correct global distinct count, the leader would need to know
which
users each worker saw, because a user that appears in worker 1's slice and again in worker 2's slice must be counted once, not twice. A partial count of distinct values cannot be combined. You would have to ship the entire set of distinct values from every worker and union them. At which point you have moved all the data to one place anyway, which is exactly what parallel aggregation exists to avoid.
An aggregate carrying
DISTINCT
(or an inner
ORDER BY
) therefore cannot run in partial mode, the planner cannot place a Partial Aggregate under a Gather, and with no partial aggregate to feed, a parallel scan buys nothing. The whole plan collapses to serial.
I checked this against PostgreSQL 17.10, 18.4, and 19beta1: partial aggregation still does not cover distinct and ordered aggregates on any of them.

data.title: What is a product?
data.author: rogix
data.article_summary:
这篇文章探讨了AI工具泛滥带来的一个现象:许多人用AI快速创建看似完整的"产品",但实际上只是原型或演示。

作者指出,尽管AI模型不断进化,网络上充斥着精美的设计原型,但四年过去了,并没有看到真正用AI创建出能与YouTube、Instagram等巨头竞争的产品。

**核心观点**:原型不等于产品。真正的产品需要具备三个要素:真实用户、真实市场、解决真实问题。用AI在几小时内搭建出Instagram的基本功能,如果没有人使用或关心,那它就不是产品,只是个玩具。

文章提醒读者不要被网上的AI演示迷惑,也不必因为没有用AI做出惊人成果而焦虑——因为真正有价值的产品依然很难构建,几乎没有人真正做到。

• **产品定义争议**：
  - 用户规模派：产品需要真实用户和市场（原文观点）
  - 问题解决派（galgantar）：产品应该看是否有能力解决真实问题，而非用户数量
  - 交换价值派（MomsAVoxell）：产品的本质是可交换性，发生交易才算产品

• **网络效应壁垒**（ngruhn, hahahaa）：AI虽能快速克隆Instagram、LinkedIn等产品，但无法复制其网络效应和用户生态，这才是真正的护城河

• **分发难题**（firasd）：AI降低了开发门槛但营销分发依然困难，获取第一个用户或第一美元并未变容易

• **实用主义**（TrackerFF）：企业用LLM自建工具替代昂贵SaaS，AI价值在降低开发成本而非颠覆市场

• **怀疑论**（batuhandumani, cengen）：AI产出多为缺乏原创性的克隆品，竞争者虽多但执行力参差，本质未改变

补充讨论：多位评论者指出AI解决了"如何构建"的问题，但产品成功的关键——市场定位、用户获取、持续运营——依然是难题

49202690.article_content:
black road bike
Photo by
Mikkel Bech
on
Unsplash
I've seen, and probably you have seen too, far too many prototypes out there created with AI treated as products, because it is
that
easy to prompt two sentences and get something that resembles a real thing. Do you want a website to sell your old furniture? Done. You want an Instagram clone? Done. What about a full-feature LinkedIn replacement? Done. Except, it is not really done.
Every other week, Anthropic or OpenAI launches a new version of their models, and every other week, the internet is flooded with examples of what those models are capable of. Beautiful designs and prototypes fill up our feeds, giving us, simple mortals, a taste of what the future looks like, on localhost. No link needed.
I am impressed. Are you impressed? Well, you should be. But when I think about this for two seconds, I realized that four years after Sam Altman tweeted about his new chatbot, I haven't seen any real competitor of YouTube, or Figma, or Google, or Instagram created solely with AI. If this thing is so powerful, where is all the innovation? Shouldn't all of us be creating our own version of GTA 6 from our garage – I mean, our couch – at this point?
It turns out a prototype is not a product. Most of what we see on YouTube that was created by the dude, who never touched a line of code before, between two cups of coffee is not even a prototype; it's nothing. If you are generous, you can call it a demo, a draft, maybe?
A real product is hard to build. I'm not saying there aren't people out there creating useful stuff in record time. What I am saying is that you shouldn't be impressed by everything you see online. Don't feel bad if you don't have anything to show up with all the free intelligence available nowadays. Almost nobody has.
A real product has real users, a real market and solves real problems.
When I think about most of the products we use daily, like X.com or Google, I wonder why nobody has a real competitor of these things before. It was not a lack of intelligence or know-how. Many companies were created with this goal in mind, but none succeeded because a product is more than the parts that compound it.
I could prompt a basic Instagram feature in a few hours, maybe a few days, but would it mean I created a product? If nobody uses it or cares, is it still a product? What makes a product is its users. If nobody is using the thing you built, you don't have a product, you have a toy. Have fun playing with it.

这篇文章探讨了AI工具泛滥带来的一个现象:许多人用AI快速创建看似完整的"产品",但实际上只是原型或演示。

作者指出,尽管AI模型不断进化,网络上充斥着精美的设计原型,但四年过去了,并没有看到真正用AI创建出能与YouTube、Instagram等巨头竞争的产品。

**核心观点**:原型不等于产品。真正的产品需要具备三个要素:真实用户、真实市场、解决真实问题。用AI在几小时内搭建出Instagram的基本功能,如果没有人使用或关心,那它就不是产品,只是个玩具。

文章提醒读者不要被网上的AI演示迷惑,也不必因为没有用AI做出惊人成果而焦虑——因为真正有价值的产品依然很难构建,几乎没有人真正做到。

data.article_summary:
这篇文章介绍了原子钟的工作原理。现代社会的GPS导航、通信网络、金融交易等都依赖原子钟提供的精确时间。

传统时钟依靠摆锤或石英晶体振荡计时,但这些人造部件存在差异且会漂移,无法保持完美同步。而同类原子完全相同且不会磨损,能产生极其稳定的"节拍"。

原子钟利用量子物理原理工作:将单个原子分离出来,用特定频率的光波照射。当光波频率接近原子的共振频率时,原子会吸收能量并发生量子跃迁。原子钟的"滴答声"正是这些激发原子的光波。通过精确调谐光波频率至原子共振频率,可以获得比任何其他时钟稳定数十亿倍的时间基准。

Atomic Clocks
How Do Atomic Clocks Work?
Credit:
N. Hanacek/NIST
Our modern world depends on clocks that tap the secrets hidden inside atoms — the tiny building blocks of matter that make up everything from our bodies to the device you’re reading this on to the planet Earth.
If you’ve checked the time on your phone, computer or smartwatch today, you have aligned yourself with the steady, unchanging beats of atoms. If you’ve used GPS for directions or flown on a plane, atomic clocks have helped deliver you safely to your destination. If you’ve bought or sold a stock, that transaction was stamped in atomic time. If you’ve made a phone call or searched the web, you have tapped into networks synced by atoms.
But how do we use these tiny particles to tell time? To peer into atoms and extract their beats, we must wield light with extreme and exquisite precision. And we must ingeniously hack into the strange and wondrous world of quantum physics, the rules that govern the world at its tiniest scales — including inside the atom.
What, Exactly, Is a Clock?
To understand atomic time, we must first understand something about clocks.
A clock is, at its core, a marriage of two components: a mechanism that oscillates, or ticks with a steady beat, and a device that counts those beats and displays the time. For most of history, the oscillating mechanisms have been human-made objects: the swinging pendulum of a grandfather clock; the quartz crystal in your wristwatch or laptop.
Credit:
Mountain Brothers/Shutterstock
But no two pendulums or crystals are exactly alike — so neither are the ticks of time they produce. Human-made timepieces can never be perfectly in sync.
Manufactured clocks have a second problem: They drift. One tick of time is slightly different from the next, and the next, and so on. Human-made clocks are inherently unstable.
Atoms, by contrast, can create almost “perfect” beats. Atoms don’t have any manufactured parts, and they don’t wear out or slow down over time. And all atoms of a given type are identical.
Quantum physics tells us that atoms absorb and emit light waves of specific colors, or frequencies. Light waves tuned to these atomic frequencies produce ticks of time that are billions of times more stable and precise than those of any other kind of clock.
Indeed, as far as we know, atomic frequencies offer the purest, most stable beats in the universe. If another advanced civilization has evolved on a distant planet, it probably measures time using atoms, as we do.
So how do these fabulous atomic clocks work?
The Inner Life of the Atom
Atoms are all around us and inside of us. But when bound by the billions in solid objects like our bodies, atoms behave very differently than when they’re on their own. To make a clock, we must first separate and isolate individual atoms from almost everything else.
We then immerse our atoms in light. Light is nature’s way of sending energy from place to place.  It travels in the form of waves that rise and fall as they speed through space, like the alternating crests and troughs of water waves traveling across the ocean. The frequency of a light wave is the number of times it cycles from crest to trough to crest again in one second.
To turn atoms into a clock, we can’t use just any light: We need light that has been finely tuned to a special frequency known as the atoms’ resonant frequency. When the light frequency is near resonance, atoms can absorb some of the light’s energy and change their internal energy state — often called a “quantum jump.”
Credit:
J. Wang/NIST
You can find an everyday example of resonance on a playground. If you push a child on a swing only when they reach a maximum height, the child will swing higher and higher. That’s because you’ve tuned your pushing rate to the swing’s natural resonant frequency. If, on the other hand, you push at random intervals, the swing won’t go higher and might even come to a stop.
Another familiar example involves an opera singer and a wine glass. When the sound waves from the singer’s voice reach the natural resonance frequency of the glass, the glass can quickly absorb a lot of energy — and shatter.
More metaphorically, we often say an idea resonates when it seems to harmonize with something inside of us.
Now you may be wondering, what provides the steady tick in an atomic clock — and what does any of this talk about resonance and energy states have to do with telling time?

data.title: Reverse Jevons Paradox
data.author: martinhath
data.article_summary:
这篇文章探讨了杰文斯悖论及其反向效应。杰文斯悖论指当资源成本下降时,总支出反而上升,因为低成本激发了更多使用和新的使用场景。例如汽油降价后人们更频繁开车,或测试套件加速后每次提交都运行。

作者提出"反向杰文斯悖论":当资源成本上升到一定程度,总支出可能降至零。例如在软件开发中,如果代码变更流程过于繁琐(多层审核、复杂流程),小型重构PR的成本变得过高,开发者会完全停止这类改进。这不是速度变慢,而是某类活动的彻底消失,对代码库健康极为不利。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：文章提出"反向杰文斯悖论"概念（成本上升导致总支出下降），引发了关于这是否为有效经济学概念的争论，以及其在软件工程中的体现。

不同观点：

• **基本经济学派**：jihadjihad、raincole等认为这只是需求法则的基本表现，不需要创造新术语。raincole质疑这是否为讽刺文章，因为结论过于直观。

• **概念澄清派**：nbernard指出作者混淆了概念——真正的杰文斯悖论是指效率提升反而导致资源使用增加，而不是简单的供需关系。pu_pe补充说杰文斯悖论之所以称为"悖论"是因为其反直觉性。

• **实践应用派**：alexpotato、xg15、cubefox通过软件工程实例说明"成本过高抑制行为"的现象——繁重的审查流程、Jira票据系统等会扼杀小型改进。cubefox特别指出，争论某项改进是否值得的会议成本往往超过直接实施的成本。janpeuker讽刺性地将此现象称为"谷歌式软件工程"。

• **普遍现象观察派**：greenfish6、geraneum认为这种"反向效应"普遍存在于住房监管、大型组织流程、繁琐表单等场景中，实质就是"官僚主义"或"繁文缛节"的体现。

补充讨论：smitty1e将讨论延伸到税收政策领域，而chvid、z3t4则从不同角度（内存使用、价格弹性）提出了相关但略偏离主题的观点。整体争议焦点在于：这是发现了新规律，还是只是用新术语包装了常识？

49162080.article_content:
Reverse Jevons Paradox
August 03, 2026
back to posts
Jevons paradox happens when the cost of a resource goes down, but the total spend on that resource goes up.
It sounds like the total spend should go down since the price went down, but
the decreased cost allows for
more use
within the same budget,
and opens up for new families of usage:
things that were previously net-negative because of the resource cost are all of a sudden net-positive
1
.
A typical example is old cars and gas price.
If gas is expensive, you'll take public transport to your work,
you'll bike to your friends and family,
and you'll walk to the grocery store every day so that each time it's not so heavy.
If gas prices drop, it suddenly makes sense to drive to places to save time.
You can bulk-shop, visit more remote friends and family,
and you can even get a new job with a
longer
commute, since it is now economically viable to do so.
Jevons paradox is often cited in programming, both when the cost is monetary but also when it's time.
If your build- and test suite is very slow, you might run it over night when you build
the
nightly build.
If it's really fast, there's no need to limit it to once per day, and you can do a full build and a full run of the test suite on every commit.
You can even do it locally before you commit, which means even more use.
This is not just speeding up the build and test suite, it is fundamentally different from building nightly builds.
Your CI bill, of course, increases.
This is all well known, but I've realized this effect also works in reverse:
if the cost of a resource goes
up
, the total spend on that resource can go down
.
It can even go all the way to zero!
I don't know if this has a name, so I'm calling it the Reverse Jevons paradox, even if it is less paradoxical sounding than the regular Jevons.
Say you're in charge of a big software effort.
If you make it hard to change code by requiring multiple levels of reviews,
a web of Jira tickets,
a horde of people needing to sign off,
and other red tape,
you might effectively kill a whole class of changes, like "small refactor" PRs.
The cost of making small changes to the codebase is so high that it becomes net-negative for a single developer to make the change.
It is no longer worth the effort, and so they won't do it anymore.
This is, of course, disasterous for the health of a codebase.
This too is a fundamental difference, not a marginal change of rate.
The codebase doesn't get the same stream of incremental improvements but at a slower rate,
the improvements stop coming altogether.
Thanks for reading.
Footnotes
If you pay
$1.00
to press a button, and pressing the button pays you
$0.99
, you will press the button zero times. If you get
$1.01
instead, you will press the button all the time.

data.author: RobinHirst11

data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：Framework笔记本电脑公司因Metabase数据泄露事件导致客户个人信息（姓名、地址、邮箱、电话等）被访问

不同观点：

• **第三方数据存储批评派**：lrvick、hellcow等认为公司不应将用户PII存储在SaaS平台，应该自建安全基础设施或根本不存储；parable指出分析平台和CRM工具已成为常见攻击向量，建议数据应保留在公司内部

• **Metabase信任危机派**：pelagicAustral提到这是Metabase第二次重大0-day漏洞，其前雇主已将基础设施迁回本地部署；chocolatkey分享了攻击细节，显示攻击者系统性扫描并提取数据库表

• **实际影响评估派**：aucisson_masque认为有人反应过度（"只是台笔记本电脑"），但parable强调元数据比密码更难更改；OroPla表示不知如何应对已泄露的不可变信息

• **对Framework不满派**：bravetraveler决定停止购买，cassianoleal质疑订单处理问题，edent批评Framework的赞助选择

补充讨论：尽管Framework及时通知并提供详细说明，但核心矛盾在于商业便利性（使用第三方分析工具加速业务）与数据安全之间的平衡，以及元数据泄露的长期风险难以补救。
